title: Dynamic Application Security Testing
summary: Dynamic application security testing is the automated assessment of a running application, sending crafted requests or driving a browser and analysing the responses for security weaknesses such as injection, broken authentication, insecure session handling, misconfigured headers, exposed administrative interfaces and unsafe redirects. Because it exercises the deployed artifact, DAST observes the same surfaces an attacker would, which makes it strong at finding configuration, authentication and session problems that static analysis cannot see. The trade-off is coverage and certainty in the other direction: black-box scanning only reaches what it can discover, it cannot reason about code it cannot see, and destructive or stateful techniques risk corrupting test data, so scans are usually run against a dedicated environment seeded with representative content and credentials. Authenticated scanning is the single biggest determinant of value; an unauthenticated scan of a modern single-page application typically crawls a login page and little else. For a practising engineer the operational questions are environment fidelity, credential handling, scan scope, rate limiting, and how findings are de-duplicated across runs so a repeated issue is not rediscovered as new. Pairing DAST with an API specification gives far better coverage than crawl-only scanning, and pairing it with static analysis closes the loop between code-level and runtime evidence. Common failure modes include scanning production during peak hours, scanning an environment with debug features enabled so results do not reflect production, and reporting every informational header finding as if it carried the same weight as a confirmed injection.
objectives: You will be able to explain what running the application adds over static analysis and which defect classes it uniquely exposes.
You will be able to configure an authenticated DAST scan with a safe test account, a scoped target and rate limits that protect the environment.
You will be able to evaluate environment fidelity and state why scanning a debug-enabled staging copy can produce misleading results.
You will be able to interpret a DAST report, separating confirmed findings from informational observations and scanner heuristics.
You will be able to define a de-duplication and retest process so recurring findings are tracked rather than rediscovered.
You will be able to combine API-specification-driven scanning with crawl-based scanning to improve endpoint coverage.
